title: Atopic dermatitis (atopic eczema)
subject: rheumatology-dermatology
setting: Primary care, dermatology and paediatric clinic
summary: Daily emollients for all, a topical corticosteroid matched to severity and site (mild potency on the face, short courses of potent), steroid-sparing topicals and twice-weekly proactive treatment for frequent flares, and biologics or oral JAK inhibitors for moderate to severe disease. Eczema herpeticum needs same-day aciclovir.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Itchy skin plus 3 or more of: visible flexural eczema (cheeks or extensor surfaces in children 18 months or under), previous flexural eczema, dry skin in the last 12 months, asthma or allergic rhinitis (or atopy in a first-degree relative in children under 4), onset before age 2 (not used under age 4).
In Asian, Black Caribbean and Black African children eczema may affect extensor surfaces rather than flexures, discoid or follicular patterns are more common, and redness can be hard to see.
Grade severity (clear, mild, moderate, severe) by skin signs and impact on sleep and quality of life. Flare triggers: soaps and detergents, infection, contact and inhalant allergens, heat, stress.

Bacterial infection: weeping, crusts, pustules, rapid worsening, fever. Eczema herpeticum: rapidly worsening painful eczema, clustered blisters, punched-out erosions 1 to 3 mm, fever or lethargy: an emergency.
Differentials: scabies, contact dermatitis (face, eyelids, hands), seborrhoeic dermatitis, tinea, psoriasis; new eczema in an older adult: consider drug eruption and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Diagnosis is clinical; no routine tests. Bacterial swab if infection fails to respond or recurs; viral swab (HSV PCR) for suspected eczema herpeticum.

Consider food allergy only after immediate reactions to a food, or in infants with moderate or severe eczema uncontrolled by optimal treatment, especially with colic, vomiting, altered bowel habit or faltering growth. Refer rather than start exclusion diets.
Patch testing for suspected allergic contact dermatitis (persistent facial, eyelid or hand eczema, or reactions to topical treatments).
Before systemic agents: CBC, liver and renal function, lipids (JAK inhibitors), hepatitis B and C, HIV and TB screening as appropriate.

sections.title: Topical therapy (stepped care)
items: Emollients for everyone, every day, even when skin is clear: large amounts (children 250 to 500 g weekly), smoothed on rather than rubbed in, and used as soap substitutes. Emollient bath additives are not recommended (NICE).

Topical corticosteroid once or twice daily to active areas only, by severity: mild potency for mild, moderate for moderate, potent for severe eczema. Face and neck: mild potency (moderate for 3 to 5 days in severe flares). One fingertip unit (0.5 g) covers two adult palms.

Children: no potent steroid under 12 months or very potent steroid at any age without specialist advice; from 12 months, potent steroid for no longer than 14 days and not on the face or neck. Axillae and groin: moderate or potent for 7 to 14 days only.
Frequent flares (2 or 3 a month): once controlled, apply topical steroid to problem areas on 2 consecutive days each week, or tacrolimus twice weekly; review within 3 to 6 months.

Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) are steroid-sparing for face, eyelids and flexures (strong, AAD); NICE uses them second line from age 2 with specialist advice. Transient burning is common.

Adults (AAD 2023 to 2025): ruxolitinib 1.5% cream, crisaborole, roflumilast 0.15% cream and tapinarof cream are further steroid-sparing options. Topical antihistamines, antiseptics and antimicrobials are not recommended for uninfected eczema.

sections.title: Moderate to severe disease: systemic therapy
items: Refer to dermatology when optimised topical treatment fails. Biologics (strong, AAD) with continued topicals: dupilumab (IL-4 receptor alpha, licensed from 6 months of age), tralokinumab and lebrikizumab (IL-13), nemolizumab (IL-31 receptor alpha). Conjunctivitis is common with dupilumab.

Oral JAK inhibitors (strong, AAD): upadacitinib and abrocitinib (baricitinib outside the US); rapid itch relief but boxed warnings for serious infection, MACE, thrombosis and malignancy, so screen and monitor CBC, lipids, liver enzymes, TB and hepatitis.
Narrowband UVB (conditional). Short-term ciclosporin, methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate are conditional alternatives, useful where biologics or JAK inhibitors are unavailable.
Avoid systemic glucocorticoid (conditional against) except as a brief bridge in severe flares; rebound is common.
Oral antihistamines are not routinely recommended; a 7 to 14 day trial of a sedating antihistamine may help sleep during flares in children 6 months or older (NICE).

sections.title: Infected eczema and eczema herpeticum
items: Bacterial infection in a well patient with localised signs may need no antibiotic beyond optimised emollient and steroid; for widespread infection give oral flucloxacillin (clarithromycin if penicillin allergic) for 5 to 7 days. Replace opened emollients and creams afterwards.

Eczema herpeticum: start systemic aciclovir immediately, even if localised, and refer the same day; admit children and anyone systemically unwell (IV aciclovir). Involvement around the eyes needs same-day ophthalmology review.
Suspect herpes simplex when infected eczema fails to respond to antibiotics and an appropriate topical steroid.

sections.title: Pregnancy and referral
items: Pregnancy: emollients and mild to moderate topical steroids can be used; narrowband UVB is an option; avoid JAK inhibitors, methotrexate and mycophenolate; systemic therapy only with specialist advice.
Urgent (within 2 weeks) specialist referral for children with severe eczema not responding to optimal topical therapy after 1 week, or failed treatment of infected eczema (NICE).
Refer when the diagnosis is uncertain, facial eczema fails to respond, contact allergy is suspected, flares occur 1 to 2 weeks a month, or eczema causes major sleep, school or psychological impact.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Steroid fear leading to undertreatment: explain that correctly used steroids are safe and label containers with the potency.
Stopping emollients once the skin is clear.
Treating eczema herpeticum as bacterial infection, or missing scabies.
Repeated oral steroid courses instead of referral for systemic therapy.
Unnecessary food exclusion diets in children, causing nutritional harm.

drugs.name: Hydrocortisone 1% (mild)
drugs.dose: Apply thinly once or twice daily to active eczema
drugs.notes: Face, neck and infants; mild eczema.

drugs.name: Clobetasone butyrate 0.05% (moderate)
drugs.dose: Apply once or twice daily to active eczema; 7 to 14 day courses for flares
drugs.notes: Face only for 3 to 5 days in severe flares.

drugs.name: Mometasone furoate 0.1% (potent)
drugs.dose: Apply once daily to active eczema for short courses
drugs.notes: Children 12 months and over: maximum 14 days, not face or neck. Proactive use 2 days a week for frequent flares.

drugs.name: Tacrolimus ointment
drugs.dose: 0.03% (age 2 to 15) or 0.1% (16 and over) twice daily until clear, then twice weekly as maintenance
drugs.notes: Steroid-sparing for face and flexures; burning early; avoid on infected skin.

drugs.name: Dupilumab
drugs.dose: Adults: 600 mg subcutaneously once, then 300 mg every 2 weeks; children from 6 months: weight-based dosing
drugs.notes: Conjunctivitis common; no routine blood monitoring.

drugs.name: Upadacitinib
drugs.dose: 15 mg orally once daily; 30 mg once daily in adults under 65 with inadequate response
drugs.notes: Age 12 and over (at least 40 kg: 15 mg). Screen TB and hepatitis; monitor CBC, lipids, liver enzymes; avoid in pregnancy.

drugs.name: Flucloxacillin
drugs.dose: Adults: 500 mg orally four times daily for 5 to 7 days; children: 12.5 to 25 mg/kg four times daily (maximum 500 mg per dose)
drugs.notes: Widespread infected eczema; clarithromycin if penicillin allergic.

drugs.name: Aciclovir
drugs.dose: Adults: 400 mg orally five times daily for 5 to 10 days; IV 5 mg/kg every 8 hours if systemically unwell or extensive
drugs.notes: Eczema herpeticum; adjust for renal function. Children: weight-based dosing with same-day specialist advice.
